newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks urge Berne to approve Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks urge Berne to approve Holocaust fund.

text.p: The Swiss Bankers Association urged its members on Wednesday to pay into a Holocaust memorial fund and asked the government to speed up the project being negotiated with Jewish groups.
Jewish and other critics have accused Swiss banks of sitting on accounts left by victims of Nazi genocide and say the country as a whole profited cynically from its neutral status in World War Two.

Association president George Krayer said 100 million Swiss francs ($68.5 million) donated by the country's three biggest banks this month was a first step in proving good will towards critics of Switzerland's role as a World War Two financial centre.
"Further donations from the rest of the banking sector and other companies, the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and the federal government must follow," Krayer told a news conference.
"This is a recommendation. We have no power to order our members to pay," he added.
Krayer said the association, the umbrella group for more than 400 banks in Switzerland, had just started talks with its members and had no commitments yet on payments.

He urged the Federal Council, or cabinet, to agree quickly with the World Jewish Congress and representatives of gypsies, who were also victims of the Holocaust, on how to share the running of the fund. The groups held talks in Berne this week.
"After the talks...we hope very much that the Swiss government will decide quickly, maybe even today, on the structure of the fund and its beneficieries," he said.

The three donor banks -- UBS , Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) -- asked the government to work out with Jewish organisations and other groups supporting Holocaust survivors how the fund will work.

The banks made their donation under pressure from the Jewish and other critics. But Berne has put off a decision on whether to chip in public money, although politicians close to the talks say the government intends to join in the coming months after winning broad political support for the step.
A leading nationalist politician suggested he might organise a referendum against any government money for the fund.

Christoph Blocher, a right-wing member of parliament who led a successful drive to block closer Swiss ties to the European Union in 1992, said he had no objection to banks and other companies putting their money into a Holocaust fund.
"What is difficult for me is what Berne plans to do with taxpayers' money," he told the national tabloid Blick.
"We must not do anything that amounts to an admission of guilt or to reparations for alleged mistakes in our trade policy (with Nazi Germany)," he added.
Asked whether he would organise a referendum against any government contribution, he said: "We will see."
Under Swiss direct democracy, any governmment policy can be challenged by referendum if 50,000 signatures are collected. ($ = 1.459 Swiss Francs)
